chunks: "When you put P-type and N-type silicon together, there's a big imbalance. The N side is full of free electrons and the P side is full of holes.
So electrons diffuse from N to P and holes diffuse from P to N, just like a drop of ink spreading, and when they cross they recombine with the other carrier.
What matters is what they leave behind. When an electron leaves the N side, it exposes a fixed positive donor ion.
When a hole leaves the P side, it exposes a fixed negative acceptor ion.
So near the junction there's a layer with no mobile carriers, only fixed charge: positive on the N side, negative on the P side. That's the depletion region.
That fixed charge creates an electric field pointing from N to P, which pushes electrons back toward N and holes back toward P. That drift opposes the diffusion.
It keeps growing until drift exactly balances diffusion, and then there's no net current. The potential across it is the built-in potential, around 0. 7 to 0.
8 volts in a typical silicon junction. Forward bias shrinks the region, reverse bias widens it, and that width is also why a reverse-biased junction behaves like a capacitor."
